Spring Boot Quickstart · Core Idea

Dependency Injection:
Drop the new Keyword

Once a class needs another object, you have a choice. It can create that collaborator itself, or Spring can provide one. Dependency Injection moves that object-creation decision outside the class that uses it.

Need a collaborator? Spring can hand it to you.
← Review IoC
🌵
💉
WANTEDLoose coupling.
Easy swaps.
Testable code.
1 · First, factor out the work

Imagine random number generation is a real service

The math is trivial here, but pretend the implementation is expensive and complicated. Maybe it calls external resources, talks to a database, or performs heavy processing. That would justify moving it into a separate collaborator.

Java · RandomNumberService
package com.mcnz.random;

public class RandomNumberService {

    public double getRandomNumber() {
        System.out.println("In the Math random number service.");
        return Math.random();
    }
}
Java · controller creates its own service
package com.mcnz.random;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
public class NumberController {

    RandomNumberService service = new RandomNumberService();

    @GetMapping("/magic-number")
    public int magicNumber() {
        int magicNumber = (int)(service.getRandomNumber() * 10);
        return magicNumber + 1;
    }

    @GetMapping("/random-number")
    public int randomNumberWithParameters(
            @RequestParam("lower-limit") int lowerLimit,
            @RequestParam("upper-limit") int upperLimit) {

        int range = upperLimit - lowerLimit + 1;
        return (int)(service.getRandomNumber() * range) + lowerLimit;
    }

    @GetMapping("/random-number/{lowerLimit}/{upperLimit}")
    public int randomNumberWithPath(
            @PathVariable int lowerLimit,
            @PathVariable int upperLimit) {

        int range = upperLimit - lowerLimit + 1;
        return (int)(service.getRandomNumber() * range) + lowerLimit;
    }
}
🔩

The coupling is hiding in one line

new RandomNumberService() means the controller chooses the concrete implementation for itself. If the implementation changes, the controller must change too.

2 · The boss changes the rules

Dev needs a cheaper implementation

Now imagine production can use one implementation, but local development should use a cheaper alternative. In plain Java, we can create another implementation and manually change which class gets instantiated.

Java · alternate implementation
package com.mcnz.random;

public class SystemRandomNumberService extends RandomNumberService {

    @Override
    public double getRandomNumber() {
        System.out.println("In the System random number service.");
        return (System.currentTimeMillis() % 100000) / 100000.0;
    }
}
Java · manual implementation swap
public class NumberController {

    RandomNumberService service = new SystemRandomNumberService();

    @GetMapping("/magic-number")
    public int magicNumber() {
        // endpoint logic continues here
    }
}
Tightly coupled

Controller decides

new SystemRandomNumberService() is a hard-coded decision inside the class that consumes the service.

→
DI goal

Container decides

The controller declares what it needs. Spring selects and supplies the configured bean.

3 · Let Spring inject it

@Autowired removes the constructor call

The first version is deliberately simple. Remove the explicit new expression from the controller, then let Spring wire in a component.

Java · field injection
package com.mcnz.random;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
public class NumberController {

    @Autowired
    RandomNumberService service;

    @GetMapping("/magic-number")
    public int magicNumber() {
        int magicNumber = (int)(service.getRandomNumber() * 10);
        return magicNumber + 1;
    }
}
Java · component Spring can create
package com.mcnz.random;

import org.springframework.stereotype.*;

@Component
public class SystemRandomNumberService extends RandomNumberService {

    @Override
    public double getRandomNumber() {
        System.out.println("In the System random number service.");
        return (System.currentTimeMillis() % 100000) / 100000.0;
    }
}
🧲

What changed?

The controller still uses a RandomNumberService, but it no longer creates the object. Spring owns that creation step and supplies the dependency.

🔔

QUIZ ALERT: DI is really about testability and replaceability

Your quiz tests the benefits of controller → service → repository layering. One major payoff is that the business logic can be tested without starting a Spring web context, because a test can provide a mock or fake collaborator instead of the real one.

4 · Profiles choose an implementation

Dev, prod, and QA can each get a different bean

Profiles let Spring activate different components for different environments. The consuming controller does not need a pile of if statements to decide which implementation to create.

Java · dev profile
package com.mcnz.random;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.*;

@Component
@Profile("dev")
public class RandomNumberService {

    public double getRandomNumber() {
        System.out.println("In the Math random number service.");
        return Math.random();
    }
}
Java · prod profile
package com.mcnz.random;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.*;

@Component
@Profile("prod")
public class SystemRandomNumberService extends RandomNumberService {

    @Override
    public double getRandomNumber() {
        System.out.println("In the System random number service.");
        return (System.currentTimeMillis() % 100000) / 100000.0;
    }
}
Java · qa-testing profile
package com.mcnz.random;

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.*;

@Component
@Profile("qa-testing")
public class ThreadLocalRandomNumberService extends RandomNumberService {

    @Override
    public double getRandomNumber() {
        System.out.println("In the ThreadLocalRandom number service.");
        return ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble();
    }
}
Activate a profile in application.properties
Properties
spring.profiles.active=dev
🧠

Production design note

A cleaner production design would normally depend on an interface rather than a concrete parent class. The controller would declare the abstraction it needs, and multiple implementations could satisfy that contract.

5 · Constructor injection

The version you will usually want in production

Field injection makes the idea easy to see, but constructor injection makes the dependency explicit and makes plain unit tests very easy to write. Spring automatically uses the constructor when there is a single constructor to satisfy.

Java · constructor injection
@RestController
public class NumberController {

    private final RandomNumberService service;

    public NumberController(RandomNumberService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }
}
Field injection

@Autowired field

Compact for demonstrations, but the dependency is less obvious to ordinary Java code and is harder to supply manually in a plain unit test.

Constructor injection

Dependency is explicit

The class cannot be created without its required collaborator. Tests can simply call the constructor with a fake or mock implementation.

🎯

QUIZ ALERT: swapping a data source should not rewrite the controller

The quiz expects you to recognize that layering plus DI lets the underlying data source change, for example from an in-memory repository to Postgres, without changing the controller. The controller depends on behavior, not on how the data source is constructed.

6 · You can inject classes you do not own

@Configuration and @Bean create third-party objects

You cannot put @Component on java.util.Random because you do not own that source code. Instead, a configuration class can create the object and register it as a Spring bean.

Java · @Configuration + @Bean
package com.mcnz.random;

import java.util.*;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public Random random() {
        return new Random();
    }
}
Java · constructor receives java.util.Random
package com.mcnz.random;

import java.util.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
public class RandomController {

    private final Random random;

    public RandomController(Random random) {
        this.random = random;
    }

    @GetMapping("/random-number")
    public int getRandomNumber() {
        return random.nextInt(10) + 1;
    }
}
🧰

@Component is not the only route

You can also use configuration classes for your own types. That keeps Spring annotations out of domain classes when you want the domain model to remain framework-neutral.

7 · Quick check

Which class should choose the implementation?

Moon Boot DI Challenge

A controller needs a pricing service. You want to unit test the controller with a fake service and later swap the production implementation. Which design best supports that goal?

Dependency Injection means the consumer receives the collaborator rather than choosing and constructing it. Constructor injection makes that relationship visible, supports replacement, and is easy to test with plain Java.

9 · Seed startup data

Use CommandLineRunner to add a SourceSystem

CommandLineRunner is a Spring Boot hook that runs once after the application context starts. It is a handy place to seed starter data, create demo records, or verify that dependency injection wired your repositories correctly.

QUIZ ALERT
Remember the idea: Spring can inject not only services, but also repositories into other beans. A CommandLineRunner bean is another good example of inversion of control in action.

What this does

  • Spring starts the app and creates the repository bean.
  • Spring then runs your CommandLineRunner.
  • The runner creates a new SourceSystem object.
  • The repository saves it to the database automatically.

That means a new row is ready before you even hit the first endpoint.

Example startup seeding code

@Configuration
public class SeedDataConfig {

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner loadSourceSystem(
            SourceSystemRepository repository) {

        return args -> {
            SourceSystem system =
                new SourceSystem(
                    "REST Server",
                    "Calls /magic-number to request new values"
                );

            repository.save(system);
        };
    }
}

public interface SourceSystemRepository
        extends CrudRepository<SourceSystem, Long> {
}

Moon Boot check

Why is this a DI example?
